newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba says Spanish officials "racist, colonialist".
newsitem.headline: Cuba says Spanish officials "racist, colonialist".

text.p: Cuba again slammed the Spanish government on Thursday for what it views as interference, with a senior official calling some members of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's government racist and colonialist.

"In this new administration, it seems there are some people...with a racist, colonialist mentality," parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon told the state news agency AIN, though he added that most Spaniards, including conservatives, had a reasonable and rational attitude towards Cuba.
"It's unacceptable that there are politicians who want to treat Cuba as though it were a slave nation," he said.

Alarcon's comments were the latest in a dispute between Havana and Madrid over steady criticism by Aznar's six-month-old conservative government of President Fidel Castro and Cuba's one-party Communist political system.

"If Cubans have been able to resist the threats and attacks of the most powerful country in the world (the United States), it is absurd that the empire they (the Cubans) defeated a century ago is now trying to impose itself on them and subjugate them," Alarcon said.
Cuba gained independence from Spain in 1898.

Alarcon said Aznar's government, in its calls for reform in Cuba, was acting like a student emulating a teacher -- the United States. Washington has long pressed for change in Cuba and maintains a 34-year economic embargo on the communist-ruled island.

Tensions between Havana and Madrid erupted on Tuesday when the Cuban Foreign Ministry protested over what it called meddling in Cuban affairs and announced it was withdrawing official approval for a new Spanish ambassador.
On Thursday, Cuban authorities reduced a huge security operation around the Spanish embassy in Havana to head off any incident.
Although the embassy was still guarded by dozens of police officers and members of civil order groups, there were far fewer than on previous days.
Hundreds of police and members of civilian order groups formed tight cordons around the embassy area on Wednesday, sealing off the streets surrounding the building.
On Wednesday afternoon, a government-organised rally of students -- planned before the current row with Spain -- took place just yards (metres) from the embassy.
The demonstration is held each November 27 to mark the killing of eight medical students under Spanish rule in 1871.
